observation: Running large language model (LLM) inference over large relational datasets for batch data analytics is extremely slow and expensive: an NVIDIA L4 GPU serving Llama3-8B processes only about 6 KB of text per second, taking roughly a day to handle 15 GB of data, and processing a comparable amount of data on OpenAI's GPT-4o costs about $10K. Although LLM invocations are increasingly offered as operators on relational tables, naively sending rows in their default order to a serving backend with a prompt KV cache leads to low cache-hit rates. Real relational workloads contain repeated cell values, joined-feature repetition, popular-item reuse, and shared RAG contexts that could serve as cached prefixes; but tables also contain highly unique leading fields such as IDs or review text, and the fixed row/field order in which requests are sent critically limits how much prefix reuse is possible.

claims: High-throughput serving systems for generative LLMs use techniques such as continuous batching and page-based KV-cache management to keep GPUs busy, but they treat each request's prompt as an externally supplied fixed token sequence.

Because these systems operate at the level of already-formed requests, whether two records from a relational workload can share cached prefixes is determined upstream by the data-to-prompt pipeline that emits rows and fields.

works.title: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models
Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention

claims: Prefix caching is an established serving-side optimization for avoiding recomputation of prefill states.

SGLang's RadixAttention maintains the KV cache of prefixes observed on a stream of requests in a radix tree, and Prompt Cache precomputes attention states for reusable text modules, so requests beginning with a shared prefix pay only for the unseen suffix.

Both methods decide what to store based on prompts as submitted; neither rewrites the prompt stream to move repeated cell values, joined features, or RAG contexts ahead of unique leading fields, so prefix reuse is an opportunistic by-product of the order in which an analytics engine sends rows.

works.title: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs
Prompt Cache: Modular Attention Reuse for Low-Latency LLM Inference

claims: Recent systems offer LLM inference as relational operators: LOTUS implements semantic filters, joins, aggregations, and top-k by rendering records into LLM prompts.

The prompts produced by such semantic operators follow the tuples' order through the query plan and the fields' order in the schema, and the operators do not arrange text into shared prefixes before requests are sent to a serving backend.
As a result, a relational workload with many repeated cells and few unique leading values will nonetheless see low cache hits if request generation is left to default row and column order.

works.title: LOTUS: Enabling Semantic Queries with LLMs over Tables of Unstructured and Structured Data

solution.idea: The related work shows that the point where prefix reuse is lost is the data-to-prompt interface, not the transformer kernel. Orca and PagedAttention keep a serving backend busy but receive each request as an already formed token sequence; RadixAttention and Prompt Cache can only exploit prefixes that happen to exist in that submitted stream; LOTUS emits one prompt per tuple in the tuple order produced by the query plan and in the schema order of the relation. Consequently, a relation whose natural leading fields are unique IDs or long review texts will hide every repeated cell value, every joined dimension feature, and every shared RAG context behind those unique tokens, and no amount of serving-side cache management can recover the reuse. The solution is therefore to treat prompt generation as a relational physical-layout problem. Concretely, we introduce a prefix-aware data-to-prompt planner that exploits two degrees of freedom that the earlier systems leave unused: the order in which fields appear inside each prompt, and the order in which row requests are sent to the cache-enabled backend. The core insight is that these two orders are semantically transparent for labeled relational fields, so they can be chosen solely to turn repeated data values into actual token prefixes. Unique row IDs and other correlation-only keys should be kept as side metadata rather than rendered into the prompt at all; semantically required but highly unique free text such as review text should be moved to the tail of the prompt; repeated values, joined features, popular-item contexts, and RAG document blocks should be placed at the head of the prompt. The request stream is then physically ordered lexicographically by those head fields, so all tuples sharing a prefix are processed contiguously and the existing radix-tree or module cache sees one long common prefix followed by a short unique suffix. This directly fixes the observation: low cache-hit rates are not caused by weak cache eviction or batching but by the fact that the high-reuse relational content is hidden behind high-uniqueness leading fields and by the fact that the stream is not sorted into prefix groups. The design deliberately leaves the backend untouched; it is an upstream rewriting of the prompt stream so that SGLang-style prefix caching, Prompt-Cache-style modular reuse, and even the page-based caches of PagedAttention are presented with repeated prefixes rather than unique-first requests. The main trade-off is the added cost of profiling fields, reordering tuples, and sorting or partitioning the input relation. This is acceptable in the target regime because LLM inference is several orders of magnitude more expensive than relational shuffling, and the same sort can be reused across all operators of a workflow if the planner records the prefix layout as a physical property. We considered trying to fix this inside the serving layer by making the cache smarter, but that cannot work because the server has no schema information to identify which cell values are repeated across rows and which fields are join dimensions rather than unique facts. We also considered simply grouping requests by one popular field while leaving the schema order unchanged; that fails when two rows share a joined context but differ in that one field, because joining on a single field cannot exploit nested or multi-field commonality. We therefore solve the general problem by choosing an ordered prefix-layout over the full set of prompt fields and by ordering the tuple stream according to that layout.
solution.implementation:
The implementation is a physical layer inserted between a LOTUS-style semantic operator and an LLM serving backend that supports prefix caching, such as a backend using RadixAttention or Prompt Cache. We call this physical operator PREFIX-LOCALITY. It consumes the input relation produced by the logical semantic operator and emits requests in a cache-conscious order. The implementation has four stages.

Stage 1: profile construction. For each operator, the planner first determines the set of fields that will be rendered into the prompt. It removes from this set any field that is only a correlation key, a row ID, or an internal handle; those values are attached as response metadata so results can be mapped back to their original tuples. For the remaining fields, the planner maintains or computes a lightweight relational profile. For every candidate field f, the profile stores the value histogram count_f(v), i.e., the estimated number of tuples in the operator input that have value v in field f, and est_tokens_f(v), the estimated token length of the canonical rendered segment for f and v, using the same tokenizer as the serving model. The profile also records schema-level hints such as foreign-key relationships and dimension-table joins, but these are only hints because what ultimately matters is the observed repetition in the materialized tuple stream of the operator. If exact statistics are unavailable, the implementation samples S tuples, typically a few thousand, and scales histograms to the estimated input cardinality; values whose scaled count is below a small threshold reuse_threshold are treated as non-repeating tail fields.

Stage 2: prefix-layout optimization. The planner chooses an ordered list of prefix fields using a recursive greedy algorithm that builds an approximate prefix trie of the request stream. It maintains a set of active partitions of the input, initially containing just the whole input relation. Let active_partitions initially be {R}. While unplaced fields remain, for each remaining field f the planner computes the marginal prefix-sharing gain of placing f next:

gain(f) = sum over each active partition P of sum over each distinct value v in P.f of max(0, count_P_f(v) - 1) * est_tokens_f(v).

The first term is the number of requests after the first that would be able to reuse the rendered segment of f if all tuples with the same value v are made adjacent. The planner appends the field f with the largest positive gain to the prefix layout, removes it from the set of unplaced fields, and then splits every active partition by the canonical serialized value of f. Partitions of estimated size one are removed from the active set because no deeper prefix reuse is possible among them; their tuples will later be rendered with whatever tail fields remain. The loop repeats. When no remaining field has positive gain, or when all partitions are singletons, the remaining fields are appended as a tail in their original schema order. This greedy is not guaranteed to find the globally optimal prefix tree, but it captures the essential relational intuition: a low-cardinality field with many duplicate values and long text will be placed ahead of a unique ID, and nested repeats such as a shared RAG context followed by a joined product description will both be pulled to the front before the unique review text. The planner stops after at most field_count iterations, and the resulting layout can be cached in the query plan.

Stage 3: tuple reordering and canonical rendering. The logical operator input is physically reordered before prompts are issued. The executor adds an ORDER BY clause whose sort key is exactly the chosen prefix layout: first by the first prefix field's canonical string value, then by the second, and so on. This guarantees that tuples sharing an exact prefix are emitted as a contiguous block. If the input is too large for an in-memory sort, the executor uses an external merge sort or a two-pass hash-partition strategy: it partitions by the first prefix field, then recursively sorts each partition by the remaining prefix fields; both strategies preserve the needed contiguity. After sorting, each tuple is rendered into a prompt string deterministically. The fixed operator instruction appears at the very front, followed by the static labels and delimiters of the prefix fields, and then the tail fields. Every field is escaped so identical values always produce identical tokens; in particular, nulls, empty strings, and list-like values are serialized with the same canonical representation across all rows. The prompt for tuple t is thus a concatenation of a stable template, a shared reusable segment, and a row-specific suffix, instead of the schema-order representation that would start with the row ID.

Stage 4: cache-cooperative streaming dispatch. The sorted row stream is fed into the serving backend in the generated order. The dispatcher does not randomly sample rows or spread requests from different prefix groups across workers in a way that would defeat temporal locality. It submits requests in FIFO order over the sorted stream; when the backend itself uses continuous batching, the batches are drawn from the front of this queue, so consecutive requests are overwhelmingly from the same prefix group. Because the backend's prefix cache stores a computed prefix in a radix tree, the first request in a prefix group computes the shared prefix once, and all subsequent requests in that group hit that cache and pay only for the short unique tail. When the executor moves to the next prefix group, a new path is computed and the old group becomes a leaf that can be evicted only after all of its rows have been processed. If the backend exposes cache statistics, the dispatcher can optionally verify that the expected prefix was retained and, when it was not, issue the next few requests in smaller nested chunks; this is only a defensive optimization, not a required component.

The parts fit together as follows. The profiler in Stage 1 feeds the layout optimizer in Stage 2. The output of Stage 2 is a prompt-layout annotation and a sort-key annotation that are attached to the logical operator plan. Stage 3 executes those annotations by reordering the relation and rendering canonical prompts. Stage 4 pumps the rendered but not-yet-sent prompts into any prefix-cache-capable serving system. Because every stage is inside the relational engine, the same mechanism composes: when a semantic operator consumes a previous operator's output, the profiler recomputes a small histogram on that intermediate relation and chooses a new prefix layout, allowing repeated intermediate LLM results to also become cacheable. The key tunable parameters are reuse_threshold for ignoring near-singleton values, S for histogram sampling when full statistics are unavailable, and, optionally, max_prefix_fields to cap the prefix layout length so that no single request's cache path becomes impractically long. No changes to RadixAttention, Prompt Cache, Orca, PagedAttention, or LOTUS internals are required; the solution only rewrites the prompt stream that those systems receive.
